content: To write a manuscript, it is essential to understand that there are various types of manuscripts, ranging from fictional works to scientific treatises, each with its own formatting expectations. These expectations can vary depending on the type of manuscript, the subject field, and the preferences of the editor or publisher. However, there are some generally accepted standards for non-academic fiction and non-fiction manuscripts that can help improve your chances of making a positive impression on the editor. General Formatting Guidelines: 1. Simplicity and Consistency: Editors prefer manuscripts that are simple, familiar, and consistent in appearance. Avoid unnecessary embellishments or unique formatting styles that could distract from the content. 2. Publisher-Specific Guidelines: Always check the publisher's website for specific formatting requirements. If these are not available, you can contact the acquisitions department for clarification. In the absence of specific guidelines, adhering to general formatting principles is usually sufficient. 3. Avoid Immediate Rejection: Using common, simple, and consistent formatting reduces the likelihood of your manuscript being immediately rejected. Basic Formatting Rules: Use black text on white paper. Avoid using colored text or decorative fonts. If submitting a hard copy, use high-quality, 20-pound bond white paper. Do not staple the pages; instead, pack them neatly and securely for shipping. Choose a traditional, 12-point font such as Times New Roman, Courier, or Arial. Avoid fonts like Comic Sans or overly large or small text sizes. Double-space the entire manuscript for readability. Create margins of approximately 1 inch (2.54 cm) on all sides to allow space for editorial notes. Include a header on every page (except the title page) with your last name, the manuscript title (or keywords from it), and the page number. For example: Smith / My Manuscript / 23. Align text to the left, leaving a jagged right edge. Do not justify the text, as left-aligned text is generally more readable. If submitting electronically, save the manuscript as a PDF unless instructed otherwise. This ensures the formatting remains intact. Title Page Layout: The title page should include your full legal name (and pseudonym, if applicable), the full title of the work, your contact information, and the word count (precise or estimated). Place your legal name and contact information in the top left corner of the page. Place the word count in the top right corner. Center the title halfway down the page in all capital letters. Below the title, include your name or pseudonym as you want it to appear on the work. At the bottom of the page, you may include copyright information and/or contact details for yourself or your agent, if relevant. Chapter Formatting: Start each chapter on a new page. Leave the top third of the page blank, except for the header. One-third of the way down the page, center the chapter number and title in all caps (e.g., CHAPTER 1 — THE BEGINNING). Begin the text of the chapter four to six lines below the title. Do not indent the first paragraph of each chapter. Indent all subsequent paragraphs and lines of dialogue, except for the first paragraph of a chapter or after a section break. Additional Components: Clearly indicate the end of the manuscript by centering the word END in all caps on the final page. For manuscripts with scenes (e.g., plays or movie scripts), use a blank line with a centered hashmark () to indicate scene breaks. If using footnotes or endnotes, maintain consistency throughout the manuscript. Endnotes are preferable if the notes consist solely of citations. Using a Word Processor (e.g., Google Docs): 1. Page Setup: Click the File tab and select Page Setup. Set the top, bottom, left, and right margins to 1 inch (2.54 cm). Ensure the document is in portrait mode. 2. Alignment, Spacing, and Font: Use left alignment with a jagged right edge (default setting). Set line spacing to Double using the line spacing button. Choose a 12-point font, preferably Times New Roman, unless otherwise directed. 3. Header Setup: Click the Insert tab and select Page Number. Choose the option that places the page number in the top right corner, excluding the title page. Add your header (e.g., Smith / My Manuscript / 1) to the left of the page number. Tips: Always review the submission guidelines of the agent or publisher to whom you are submitting your manuscript. They may have specific requirements. Academic manuscripts often follow field-specific formatting styles, such as MLA for humanities, Chicago for history and journalism, APA for social sciences, and individual style guides for hard sciences. Use spellcheck and proofread thoroughly. Reading the manuscript in reverse order (starting with the last chapter) can help catch errors. Warnings: Do not attempt to make your manuscript stand out by using unique or unconventional formatting. This will likely frustrate the editor. Avoid manipulating font size or width to alter the length of your manuscript. Editors are adept at recognizing such tactics. By adhering to these guidelines, you can ensure that your manuscript is professional, readable, and well-received by editors and publishers.
